title: Lynx and Hares: Predators and Prey
subject: life science
goal: Find out how the numbers of a predator and its prey change together over many generations, and explain why.
materials: one sheet of plain paper for the forest
steps: One sheet of paper is the forest. Spread 4 hares on it, not touching, and put 1 lynx beside it. Record generation 0.
The lynx hunt: drop each lynx card on the forest from about a foot up. Every hare it touches is eaten. Take those hares off.
A lynx that ate 3 or more hares survives and has one young: add a lynx. A lynx that ate fewer starves: take it away. If no lynx are left, 1 moves in from another forest.
Every hare left has one young: double the hares, up to 60 (the forest can't feed more). Spread them out again.
Record the hares and lynx, then do the next generation.
listen_for: Noticing that lynx numbers rise after hare numbers rise, not at the same time.
“The lynx ate all the hares” when hares crash: ask what happened to the lynx next, and why.
The Skeptic asking whether one toss can prove anything, or whether the pattern repeats.
debrief: Have Reporters call out their numbers; sketch two or three groups' hares and lynx on the board. Ask: which rises first? Which falls first?

Fur-trade records from Canada show the same up-and-down pattern about every 10 years (the worksheet graphs them). Ask: those count furs sold, not animals alive. What could make the counts differ from the real numbers? And what's missing from our card model?
sources: A classic predator-and-prey card toss, rewritten for Paper Loop; computer models such as NetLogo's Wolf Sheep Predation (Wilensky, Northwestern University) explore the same idea. The worksheet's data are Hudson's Bay Company fur records, 1900-1920, as compiled by ecologists (thousands of furs).
